title: HIS-201 Ch. 3 — 1 Definitions
subject: HIS-201
topic: Chapter 3: Colonization and Conflict in the South

cards.def: The Algonquian title for a paramount chief who gathered villages into a confederacy and received their tribute in return for protection and leadership.
The economic theory that a nation grows rich by regulating trade, exporting more than it imports, and using colonies to supply raw materials and buy finished goods.
A business owned by many investors who pool their money by buying shares, so each shares in the profits and limits his own risk.
A land policy that granted acres of colonial land to each settler and to any sponsor who paid an immigrant's passage.
A laborer bound by contract to work for a master for a fixed term of years in exchange for passage across the Atlantic.
A colony granted by the Crown to an individual or family, the proprietor, who controlled its land and government.
A colony governed directly by the Crown through a royal governor rather than by a private company or proprietor.
An annual land rent that settlers in a proprietary colony owed to the proprietor for the use of their land.
A series of English laws that reserved colonial shipping for English ships and forced key colonial exports and imports to pass through England.
Colonial products listed in the Navigation Acts that colonists were allowed to ship only to England or other English colonies.
A religious settlement where Catholic priests lived among Indians in order to convert them and make them obedient Christian farmers and artisans.
The Atlantic voyage that carried enslaved Africans to the Americas below deck in overcrowded, violent, and deadly conditions.
The dangerous first period after arrival during which enslaved Africans faced new diseases, forced labor, and cultural displacement in America.
A colonial law that restricted enslaved people's movement, rights, and family life and enforced the power of masters and racial hierarchy.
An economy devoted to producing a single profitable staple crop for export, which concentrates land, labor, wealth, and power.
A South Carolina stock-raising farm where enslaved cowboys let cattle range freely across the open countryside.
Tribute was the payment of food, furs, and skins that Powhatan collected from confederacy villages in return for alliance, patronage, and protection.
A subject king was the status English colonists tried to impose on Powhatan by crowning him under James I, a crown they had to force onto his head.
The starving time was the Jamestown winter of 1609 to 1610, when hunger and disease left only sixty survivors, some of whom ate corpses.
A favorable balance of trade, the mercantilist goal, meant a nation's exports exceeded its imports so that gold and silver flowed home.
Secularization was the conversion of central Mexican Franciscan missions into self-supporting parishes by the 1570s, which pushed Franciscans toward frontier conversion work.
A coffle was a forced march of African captives linked by chains or wooden yokes from the interior to coastal slave forts.
Maroon communities were settlements of escaped enslaved Africans who fled plantations and lived beyond their masters' control in the Americas.
Manumission was a master's freeing of an enslaved person, which late-seventeenth-century Virginia laws made much harder to obtain.
Buccaneers were English raiders who traded illegally with Spanish settlements, sacked coastal towns, and attacked Spanish silver ships from Caribbean bases.
Subtleties were elaborate sugar sculptures served at medieval court feasts, when European elites treated sugar as a costly spice and medicine.
Naval stores were the masts, pitch, tar, and turpentine that North Carolina produced alongside general farming because poor harbors limited its markets.
The worthy poor were the industrious, Protestant European paupers whom Georgia's trustees recruited to become small farmers, rather than inmates of debtors' prisons.
Ashkenazim were German Jews and Sephardim were Spanish and Portuguese Jews, and both groups established a Jewish community in Savannah, Georgia.
The sickle-cell trait was an inherited condition that gave Africans more resistance to malaria than Europeans, though they remained vulnerable to respiratory infections.
Mestizos were people of mixed Spanish and Indian ancestry and mulattoes of mixed Spanish and African ancestry, both part of New Mexico's colonial population.
